EICMA 2026 • Honda Africa Twin Gets Biggest Refresh in a Decade, They Now Call It CRF1150L
Richard Petty's Daytona Boss 429 Powered This One-of-One 1970 Mustang Tasca Drag Racer, 3,000 Miles
85 photos
Photo: Bring A Trailer/HPHS81
"My father said, 'See that carbon on those pistons? That's Daytona carbon!' That Boss 429 was totally set up. I took Edsel Ford II for a ride one afternoon on the back roads. When I hit second gear the seat track broke and Edsel ended up in the back seat, but I just kept on going." Carl Tasca’s one-of-a-kind 1970 Ford Mustang Boss 429 drag race car would shut down everything else going on around it, no matter where it should happen to show up. And that’s saying something, since any Boss Nine, even the most run-of-the-mill example, is an event in itself.
First of all, allow me to express my deepest and most sincere sympathy for those who think the Ford Mustang Boss 429 is extraordinary, over-the-top, king of the hill, top of the heap, Big Boss. Well, truth be told, that last one isn’t exactly all that hyperbolizing of a descriptor, is it? I mean, it’s literally the car’s name. What more of an in-your-face sobriquet could it have? Well, here’s a suggestion, If I may "Petty Tasca."
Few names in American muscle car lore – particularly Blue Oval fan clubs – command the immediate reverence of Tasca Ford and Petty Enterprises. Virtually anything with ties to either of those two grand establishments will have gearheads listen, watch, and investigate with serious dedication.
Naturally, this one-off 1970 Ford Mustang Boss 429 currently up for grabs on Bring a Trailer unites both dynasties under one bulging fiberglass hood. And that’s not a metaphor – just scroll through the gallery and see the mountain hump laying claim over entire parcels of hood real estate.
Photo: Bring A Trailer/HPHS81 What separates this Grabber Blue fastback from the rest of the blue-chip collector pack is not untouched showroom originality, but a documented pedigree forged in factory-backed motorsport. Assigned Kar Kraft serial number 2124, Boss 429 #0F02Z109082 was delivered new to Bob Tasca’s famed dealership in East Providence, Rhode Island, where it was immediately drafted into straight-line combat rather than prepped for delivery to a wealthy high-octane addict.
Original factory paperwork confirms that this mean Mustang was invoiced on September 9, 1969, and cleared the Dearborn Assembly Plant Driveaway Garage on September 12, 1969, at 8:26 AM. Routed through Shelby and Kar Kraft under special order code DSO 89 2500, the Mustang was billed to Tasca Ford Sales at 777 Taunton Avenue in East Providence, Rhode Island, for $4,137.69.
If that seems suspiciously cheap , it is: the sticker price for retail customers was $5,107.95. However, Ford Division of Ford Motor Company invoiced the dealer at wholesale price, for obvious reasons. The wholesale bill gave Tasca Ford a gross paper margin of $970.26 – a 24% markup, if you care for bookkeeping.
Photo: Bring A Trailer/HPHS81 According to its Dearborn broadcast sheet, the nefarious pony car left the factory in Grabber Blue paint over White Corinthian vinyl high-back bucket seats. It carried the Drag Pack 3.91:1 rear axle, Competition Suspension, power front disc brakes, power steering, a console, a Rim-Blow steering wheel, an AM radio, the Decor and Convenience Check groups, an 8,000-rpm tachometer, a round clock, and a set of F60x15 raised-white-letter tires with no collapsible spare.
Few dealerships on earth could match the performance credentials of Tasca Ford, where patriarch Bob Tasca coined the motto "Win on Sunday, Sell on Monday" and fathered the 428-cubic-inch Cobra Jet. Period dealership records show Tasca sold seven 289 Shelby Cobras, six 427 Shelby Cobras, 162 Shelby Mustangs, 14 Boss 302s, six Boss 351s, seven 429 Super Cobra Jets, and nine Boss 429s, including this Grabber Blue 1970 fastback - Carl Tasca’s racer. Name no coincidence, in case you’re wondering.
Rather than racing the stock Z-code big-block V8 , Bob’s son and general manager, Carl Tasca, orchestrated a legendary engine swap. During the 1969 NASCAR season, Richard Petty briefly left Plymouth to campaign a Ford Torino Talladega in car number 43, winning nine races before returning to Mopar. As Carl Tasca recounted in the book “Boss Mustang: 50 Years” by Donald Farr, he acquired the Boss 429 V8 from Petty’s Daytona car.
Photo: Bring A Trailer/HPHS81 Carl Tasca vividly remembered driving to the Railway Express station in Lincoln, Rhode Island, to pick up the crated Petty Enterprises race motor for his second Boss 429, Kar Kraft 2124. Once back at the East Providence dealership, Tasca mechanics Bill Gilbert and John Healey pulled the aluminum cylinder heads off the block, prompting Bob Tasca to point at the pistons and exclaim that they still wore genuine Daytona carbon.
Keen-eyed gearheads will immediately raise an eyebrow, for good reason: Petty won the February 1969 Daytona 500 with a 427 V8 before the Boss 429 made its competition debut on March 31, 1969. The very first official NASCAR race featuring the legendary Boss 429 engine was the Atlanta 500 on March 30, 1969, held at the Atlanta Motor Speedway.
It was a dream debut for Ford's new powerplant, as it won the race on its very first outing. Cale Yarborough took the checkered flag driving a Mercury Cyclone prepped by the famous Wood Brothers racing team. Eventually, the Boss 429 race engine would sweep the season with 26 victories, bringing the 1969 championship cup over in Ford’s trophy room.
Photo: Bring A Trailer/HPHS81 Petty’s Talladega also raced the July 1969 Firecracker 400 at Daytona, and tested Boss 429 hardware extensively. It’s still a Daytona race, regardless of the exact date; Tasca Ford crowned Petty’s engine with a Weiand tunnel-ram intake, dual Holley four-barrel carburetors, and four-into-one headers.
Beneath the hand-cut hood scoop sat the 7.0-liter V8 featuring four-bolt main caps, forged steel internals, and aluminum cylinder heads with crescent-shaped combustion chambers and staggered valves. Basically, a semi-hemi, and the canted valves required oversized heads, leaving no room for anything else in the bay.
Fed by a single 735-cfm Holley four-barrel carburetor and breathing through a 10.5:1 compression ratio, the street engine was conservatively rated at 375 hp at 5,200 rpm and 450 lb-ft of torque at 3,400 rpm, though uncorked dynos revealed over 500 hp.
Photo: Bring A Trailer/HPHS81 Determined to dethrone Chrysler’s dominant 426 Hemi on NASCAR superspeedways, Ford developed a semi-hemispherical 429-cubic-inch V8, nicknamed the Blue Crescent. Because NASCAR rules mandated that at least 500 engines and host vehicles be sold to the public, Ford chose the Mustang to carry its new big-block weapon.
Produced across two model years, the Boss 429 saw 859 examples built for 1969 and 499 units completed for 1970, bringing the total run to 1,358 cars. Every single example left the line in the two-door SportsRoof fastback body style. Because the standard Mustang engine bay at Ford’s Dearborn assembly plant could not swallow the massive 429-cubic-inch block, unfinished cars were shipped to Kar Kraft in Brighton, Michigan.
Inside Kar Kraft’s facility at 800 Whitney Road, technicians hand-modified each Mustang by cutting and widening the front shock towers, beefing up the suspension with oversized spindles, and relocating the battery to the trunk. The resulting package carried a base price of $4,798 in 1969 and $4,918 in 1970, easily eclipsing the $5,000 mark with options and costing nearly double the price of a base Mustang SportsRoof fastback.
Photo: Bring A Trailer/HPHS81 The Boss 429 V8 alone was $1,208 retail price; Tasca was invoiced $955 for this Grabber Blue unit and its original motor. Every factory Boss 429 channeled its output through a close-ratio TopLoader four-speed manual transmission paired with a 3.91:1 Traction-Lok rear axle.
Choked by a small carburetor and saddled with street-biased Goodyear Polyglas GT tires, a stock example tested by Car Life in July 1969 sprinted from 0 to 60 mph in 7.1 seconds and cleared the standing quarter-mile in 14.09 seconds at 102.85 mph, begging for race-shop liberation. Which Tasca Ford had every intention of doing.
To clear the towering dual-quad induction setup, the dealership fabricated a domed lift-off hood secured by exposed pins, adding white hockey-stick stripes (you might have seen those on the other Boss Mustang of the period, the small-block 302 V8 “Son of Trans Am”), a white tail panel, gigantic traction bars, rear chassis reinforcements , a driveshaft safety loop, and 15-inch American Racing magnesium wheels.
Photo: Bring A Trailer/HPHS81 The setup hit so violently that when Carl Tasca took Edsel Ford II for a back-road ride and slammed second gear, the passenger seat, dumping Edsel into the back.
After Carl Tasca campaigned KK 2124 at northeastern drag strips and logged roughly 3,000 miles, the dealership retired the bruiser. A State of Connecticut tax form and sales paperwork from Tasca Lincoln-Mercury document the sale of the Mustang on September 30, 1974, to drag racer Henry E. Austin, Jr. for $4,500 cash, explicitly stipulating a race engine for race use only.
Operating out of Norwich, Connecticut, Henry E. Austin, Jr. raced the Petty-powered Mustang throughout the 1970s while carefully maintaining its Ford hardware . Invoices from Simon Ford in Norwich dated February 29, 1980, billed to Austin’s Amoco station, show him ordering a factory front spoiler, door weatherstrips, quarter-window moldings, and fuel tank components. An October 14, 1990, letter from registrar Steve Strange even referenced Austin’s vintage tractor-trailer race rig.
Photo: Bring A Trailer/HPHS81 Purchased by its current owner in 2014 after decades in storage, Kar Kraft 2124 underwent a exterior refinish in factory Grabber Blue by Randy DeLisio at DeLisio’s Performance in Lyons, New York, in 2015. Meanwhile, its Petty Enterprises NASCAR V8 was shipped to George’s Speed Shop in Dayton, Ohio, where International Drag Racing Hall of Fame legend "Ohio” George" Montgomery personally performed a $6,125 rebuild and dyno session.
Montgomery’s itemized invoice lists eight new pistons, connecting rods, a modified and balanced crankshaft, a roller-lifter camshaft, new valves, and oil restrictors to keep the Petty mill singing. Showing just 3,300 miles on its odometer and offered on a bill of sale with its original build sheet, factory invoice, and historical records, this one-of-one Tasca Petty Mustang Boss 429 is an irreplaceable monument to factory drag racing. It is also for sale.
The car is listed on Bring A Trailer, with the current bid standing at $150,500 (after less than 24 hours since the listing went live), and with six days left for prospects to place their bets. I know this is going to be high-dollar, but all I’m asking is your two cents’ worth in the comments: what’s this majestic unicorn’s correct price?
Via // Bring A Trailer
